implementation_notes: JavaScript makes the pattern a language contract instead of a class pair: an object is iterable when it has a [Symbol.iterator]() method returning an iterator (a next() method returning { value, done }), and for-of, spread, destructuring, Map/Set constructors and Promise combinators all dispatch through it, so the client never sees the storage. Implement the protocol on the collection and return a fresh iterator per call so the collection stays replayable, and honour the optional return()/throw() hooks that built-in syntax calls on early exit (break, destructuring shortfall) for cleanup.
pitfalls: next() must return an object; returning a primitive makes every built-in iteration throw TypeError ('iterator.next() returned a non-object value').

Iterators obtained from one collection are independent, but a generator or a self-returning iterator is single-use: spreading a spent iterator silently yields nothing, and a non-well-formed iterable fails late at the use site.
Cleanup is opt-in: built-in syntax only calls return() if the iterator defines it, and wrapper iterators must forward return()/throw() to the inner iterator (yield* does this for you).

variants.name: Generator functions
variants.idiom_name: function* yielding values (Generator implements iterator + iterable protocol)
variants.implementation_notes: Generator functions replace hand-written cursors: calling a function* returns a Generator that implements both the iterator and the iterable protocols, each yield suspends the body with its local state preserved, and the traversal reads as linear code - including recursive and stateful algorithms that are painful to express as an explicit cursor. Generators are single-use and bidirectional (next/throw/return, with values passed into next() becoming the result of the suspended yield). Async sources take the async function* form, which yields through Symbol.asyncIterator and is consumed with for await.
pitfalls: A generator is consumed once: iterating the same object twice yields nothing on the second pass, and the value passed to next() becomes the result of the corresponding yield (the first call's argument is always ignored).
Errors thrown inside the generator surface at the next()/iteration site and finish the generator; wrapper iterators must forward throw()/return() unless they use yield*.
Async generators resolve a promise per step, so mixing for-of with an async iterable throws TypeError; use for await, and remember that each yielded promise's rejection rejects the iteration result.
